Write-Through / Write-Back Cache

Two write strategies for a cache backed by a persistent store. Write-Through: writes to cache AND store simultaneously (consistent, slower). Write-Back: writes to cache only, flushes to store later (faster, risk of data loss). Interview favorite for system design crossover.
Hard Amazon · Google System Design crossover
get() O(1) put() O(1) cache flush() O(dirty)
Concept
Implementation
Interview
1

Two Write Strategies

Write-Through

Every write goes to both cache and backing store simultaneously.

  • + Data always consistent
  • + No data loss risk
  • - Higher write latency (2 writes)
  • - Store is bottleneck

Write-Back (Write-Behind)

Writes go to cache only. Dirty entries flushed to store later.

  • + Lower write latency
  • + Can batch flushes
  • - Risk of data loss before flush
  • - More complex (dirty tracking)
2

3

Read Path — Same for Both

get(key)

  1. Check cache → if HIT, return value (O(1))
  2. If MISS → read from backing store
  3. Populate cache with fetched value
  4. Return value

Both strategies have the same read path. The cache absorbs reads regardless of write policy.

Fields

private final Map<K, V> backingStore = new HashMap<>();  // simulated DB
private final Map<K, V> cache = new HashMap<>();
private final Map<K, Boolean> dirty = new HashMap<>();   // for write-back
private final int capacity;
private final boolean writeBack;  // true = write-back, false = write-through
2

get(key) — read-through

public V get(K key) {
    // Check cache first
    if (cache.containsKey(key)) {
        System.out.println("  [Cache HIT] " + key);
        return cache.get(key);
    }
    // Cache miss — read from backing store
    V value = backingStore.get(key);
    if (value != null) {
        System.out.println("  [Cache MISS] " + key + " — loaded from store");
        cache.put(key, value);
    }
    return value;
}
3

put(key, value) — write-through vs write-back

public void put(K key, V value) {
    if (writeBack) {
        // Write-Back: cache only, mark dirty
        cache.put(key, value);
        dirty.put(key, true);
    } else {
        // Write-Through: write to BOTH cache and store
        cache.put(key, value);
        backingStore.put(key, value);
    }
}
4

flush() — write-back only

public void flush() {
    for (K key : dirty.keySet()) {
        backingStore.put(key, cache.get(key));
    }
    dirty.clear();
}
In a real system, flush() would be called periodically by a background thread, on eviction, or on graceful shutdown to prevent data loss.

Common Follow-ups

What about Write-Around?

Write-Around: writes go directly to the store, bypassing the cache. Cache is only populated on read (read-through). Good for write-heavy workloads where data isn't read immediately after writing. Avoids cache pollution.

How to prevent data loss in write-back?

  • Write-Ahead Log (WAL) — log dirty writes to disk before acknowledging
  • Replication — replicate the cache across nodes
  • Periodic flush — flush every N ms or every K dirty entries
  • Flush on eviction — when a dirty entry is evicted, flush it first

Real-world examples?

SystemStrategy
CPU L1/L2 CacheWrite-through (to L3) or write-back with dirty bit
OS Page CacheWrite-back (dirty pages flushed by pdflush/kswapd)
SSD FTLWrite-back (NAND pages, garbage collection)
Redis + MySQLWrite-through (app writes both) or write-behind (async)
CDNWrite-around (origin push) or read-through (on miss)

Cache Invalidation?

"There are only two hard things in CS: cache invalidation and naming things."

Strategies: TTL-based (combine with TTLCache), event-driven (pub/sub on DB changes), versioning (ETag/Last-Modified). Write-through avoids the worst invalidation problems since cache and store are always in sync.

3

Edge Cases & Gotchas

Crash before flush — Write-back's biggest risk. If the process crashes, all dirty entries are lost. This is why databases use a WAL even with a buffer pool (which is essentially a write-back cache).
Eviction of dirty entries — If using write-back with an LRU eviction policy, you MUST flush a dirty entry before evicting it. Otherwise you silently lose the write.
Batch flushes — Write-back can batch multiple writes into a single store operation (e.g., bulk INSERT). This amortizes the store write cost and is why write-back throughput can be much higher.
